failures.text: About 26% of your pay goes to tax now; about 15% in retirement. Now, federal, state and payroll tax take about $74,000 of your $286,000 pay. You are 58 and plan to retire at 66, so three rules matter most now. Catch-up rule: if you are 50 or older and in a 401(k), you can contribute more than the basic limit each year. For 2027 the general catch-up is $8,500, and it rises to $11,750 at ages 60 to 63, which covers you for the next few years. The IRA limit stays at $7,500 with a $1,100 catch-up. Medicare at 65: Medicare generally starts when you turn 65, and your 7-month sign-up window runs from 3 months before to 3 months after that birthday. You plan to retire at 66, so you will need to sign up for Medicare at 65 even if you keep working, or you may face a late penalty that grows the longer you wait. Social Security: you can claim as early as 62, but you get full benefits only at full retirement age. Benefits rise for each month you delay past full retirement age, up to age 70. Waiting until 66 means you will be past full retirement age if you were born in 1959 or later, or close to it, so check your own full retirement age on the SSA site.
